drug_class: Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) — a type of antiretroviral medicine
purpose: Etravirine is used to treat HIV-1 infection in adults and children. It is always used in combination with other HIV medicines, never on its own. It helps control HIV so your immune system can stay stronger and healthier.
how_it_works: HIV needs a special tool called reverse transcriptase to make copies of itself inside your body. Etravirine blocks this tool, so the virus cannot reproduce as easily. By slowing down how fast HIV multiplies, the medicine helps keep your viral load low and protects your immune system.
common_side_effects: The most common side effect is a skin rash, which usually appears in the first few weeks and often goes away on its own. You may also experience nausea, diarrhea, stomach pain, headache, or tiredness. Most of these side effects are mild, but let your doctor or pharmacist know if anything bothers you.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you develop a severe rash, especially if it comes with fever, blisters, mouth sores, or eye redness — this can be a sign of a serious skin reaction. Etravirine can interact with many other medicines, so always tell your healthcare team everything you are taking, including vitamins and herbal supplements like St. John's Wort, which can make etravirine stop working. Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first.
typical_dosing: The usual adult dose is two 200 mg tablets (400 mg total) taken twice a day, after a meal. Taking it with food is important because it helps your body absorb the medicine properly. Your doctor may adjust the dose for children based on their weight.
